messages.subject: Penalized splines using INLA (Canadian Age Income Data)
messages.subject_clean: Penalized splines using INLA (Canadian Age Income Data)
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm new to INLA and trying to fit a penalized splines model of degree 2,  to model Canadian Age Income Data as described in section 3  of Bayesian Analysis for Penalized Spline Regression Using WinBUGS <http://people.orie.cornell.edu/davidr/papers/nonparametricbayes2.pdf> by Ciprian M. Crainiceanu, David Ruppert and M.P. Wand.

I have create design matrices  for fixed effects and random effects  as described in the original reference. And I used age.income data set in SemiPar package

data(age.income)
ageIncome <- age.income
knot=c(23,24,25,27,30,32,35,38,40,42,46,49,52,55,59)
nknots = 15

# Create fixed effects matrix
ageIncome <- cbind(ageIncome,row.names(ageIncome))
names(ageIncome)[3] <- "obsn"
ageIncome[,3] <- as.numeric(ageIncome[,3])
ageIncome[,4] <- ageIncome[,1]^2
names(ageIncome)[4] <- "age2"

#Create random effects matrix Z
Z <- matrix(NA,nrow=n,ncol=nknots)
u <- Z

for (i in 1:n)
{
  for (k in 1:nknots)
  {
    u[i,k]<-(covariate[i]-knot[k])*step(covariate[i]-knot[k])
    Z[i,k]<-pow(u[i,k],degree)
  }
}

Here the code segment I used for fit the model using INLA
formula <- log.income ~ age + age2 +f(obsn,model='z',Z=Z,hyper='gamma',param=c(.001, 0.001))

inla.fit  <-  inla(formula,data=ageIncome, family="gaussian", control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE) )

summary(inla.fit)

plot(ageIncome$age,ageIncome$log.income,xlab="age",ylab="log(Income)")
lines(ageIncome$age,inla.fit$summary.fitted.values[,1],col='red')

However, I'm unable to get  the expected results. Could you please help me to pin point in the mistake I have done here. I'm using INLA stable version (0.0-1404466487).

Thanks in Advance.

Mahasen Dehideniya

Summary of the model

messages.subject: Comparing likelihoods for point process with different meshes
messages.subject_clean: Comparing likelihoods for point process with different meshes
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I came across a frustrating little problem. I've been running point process models, and wanted to compare different meshes (in particular, whether adding more integration points improved the marginal likelihood). What I found was that the likelihood decreased as I added integration points. The reason for this is simply that INLA doesn't see what the model really is, and treats the integration points as data, so includes them in the likelihood.

So, can anyone suggest how to calculate the marginal likelihood just for the data and not the integration points? I would imagine this is the same as wanting to calculate the marginal likelihood for one likelihood in models with more than one likelihood (an issue I have too!).

Bob

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Comparing likelihoods for point process with different meshes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

unfortunately the continuous domain log-Gaussian point process
likelihood construction (using integration points, E=0,y=1 for observed
points and E=weights,y=0 for integration points) doesn't include all
the normalisation needed to get the marginal likelihood.

I'm not even entirely sure if the marginal likelihood is necessarily
well-defined or not, as it's for an infinite-dimensional object.
(Aggregating points to count data on a lattice would turn it into a
finite-dimensional problem, which behaves differently.)

It's possible that something sensible can be calculated, but I'm not
sure what that would be or how easy it would be.

Finn L

messages.body_plain:
On 08/10/14 16:30, cm...@st-andrews.ac.uk wrote:
> Hi,
> I'm attempting to define a mesh in R3 and obtain the following error
> message,
>
> fmesher.cc(793)	Points not in the plane or on a sphere, and triangulation empty.
> meshc.cc(1347)	NOT IMPLEMENTED: bool fmesh::MeshC::CET(int, double)
>
> which is clear enough, however is there an updated way with which the mesh can be defined not on a sphere? I have read a previous post entitled Re: [r-inla] Re: inla.fmesher.smorg, and can get around the problem, but I was wondering if there is a trick that I'm missing?

Hi,

no, the code doesn't support constructing 2D manifold meshes on
manifolds that are not subsets of R^2 or S^2.  The code _does_ support
building spde objects on top of such meshes, given a 2-manifold
triangle mesh constructed by some other package (rgdal I think can do
it for some situations, for example).

An already constructed triangulation can be translated by calling
   inla.mesh.create(tv=tv, loc=loc)
where loc are the 3D locations, and tv is a T-by-3 matrix of triangle-
vertex indices, in counterclockwise order within each triangle, one
triangle per row.  This is a common format, but sometimes it's in
clockwise order or in inconsistent order, in which case it needs to be
unified before calling inla.mesh.create().

The easiest way to translate from another format or to construct a
2-manifold triangulation depends on your precise problem.

Finn

messages.subject: How to model independent BYM random effects in a single model.
messages.subject_clean: How to model independent BYM random effects in a single model.
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I want to perform an ecological regression study using the model proposed by Besag, York and Mollié (BYM).

The "problem" here is that I have small areas in 33 disconnected regions and I would like to model all the small areas and regions at the same time. Therefore, I would like to use a model more or less like the following:

I will denote O_ij the number of observed cases in small area i (i=1,...,n_j) of region j (j=1,...,33), E_ij the expected number of cases, RRij the relative risk, and X_ij a covariate.

O_ij ~ Poisson(E_ij*RR_ij)
ln(RR_ij)=beta_1j + beta_2j*X_ij + S_ij + H_ij

Where,

S_ij ~ ICAR(sd1_j)     <- Spatial r.e.
H_ij ~ Normal(0,sd2_j) <- iid r.e.

i.e. I would like to take into account different variances (sd1 and s2) for each region j. Which I think that is equivalent to model independent BYM for each region.

Is it possible with INLA???

Thank you,

Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marc,

When you have disconnected components it still works. You only have
problem if you have any area isolated, with no neighbours, and wants to
scale the model, see inla.doc('bym2'), to have interpretation on the
precision parameter. Usually the correlated effects are constrained to
sum to zero at each disconnected component and it makes no sense for one
isolated area.

Best,
Elias.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Elias,

if I understand properly, when I have a graph with more than one connected compoment INLA automatically introduce a sum-to-zero constraint for each subgraph "j". However, INLA is considering the same variance (or precision) parameter for the data in each subgraph i.e. S_ij ~ ICAR(sd). For this reason, I would like to introduce more flexibility into the model by estimating a diferent variance (or precision) parameter for each disconnected component "j" i.e.  S_ij ~ ICAR(sd_j).

Today, I have tried to include independent random effects "bym" for each subgraph "j" by including NA's (i.e. 33 "bym" random effects = 33 heterogeneous effects + 33 spatial effects), but the model doesn't finish and takes memory (RAM) values ​​greater than 30GB!.

Do you know if there is another way to include different variances in each subgraph??

Thank you,

Marc

Hi,

this is controlled by the option in f(..., adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE), if
set to FALSE, then there is just one sum-to-zero constr and the
correction for disconnected subgraphs is disabled.

if you have several subgraphs with different variances, and these are
disconnected, then you have to use several f()'s, like
f(i, model="besag") + f(j, ....) + f(....)

As you say I'm using several f()'s

f(i, model="bym") + f(j, ....) + f(k,....) +...

but I have to include 33 f()'s with a mean of 300 small areas in each region!

Perhaps you are thinking why I want to estimate different variances if it is the same as performing separate models for each region. I need it because I want to perform a multilevel (or hierarchical) model, in which the first level are the small areas and the second level the regions. Thus, I want to add a iid random effect for the regions and include covariates both at small area level and at region level.

I've performed a similar model with WINBUGS and takes 6 hours. But I fear that with INLA this model takes more time and consumes a huge amount of (RAM) memory (even using Gaussian strategy). In contrast, if I analyse each region independently INLA goes faster.

Thank you for your help!

Marc

messages.subject: Using the 'T' likelihood takes forever
messages.subject_clean: Using the 'T' likelihood takes forever
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLAers,

I’m dealing with a rather large dataset (~ 250K obs.) with soil measurements by region and year.
The number of measurements in a given region and year vary a lot between 0 and a few dozens.

The goal is to fit a spatio-temporal model, but my exploratory data analysis revealed very heavy tails.
So I decided to try the ‘T’ likelihood, but it takes forever while a model with gaussian likelihood is fitted in a matter of minutes.

I simplified the model at maximum, fixed the degrees of freedom, and specified informative priors as much as possible.
But still, it never ends (up to several hours).
Here is the simplified model

I post here a minimal reproducible example, with access to the dataset.

Anything I can do about it?

Thanks!
ƒacu.-

PD: Using verbose, it looks that it is the optimisation step which takes very long.
# Download data
library(RCurl)
bin <- getBinaryURL('https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/65539579/dat.rds',
                    ssl.verifypeer = FALSE)
con <- file('dat.rds', open = "wb")
writeBin(bin, con)
close(con)

## Load  243K obs of 5 variables
dat <- readRDS(file = file('dat.rds'))

## Priors
lik.hyper <- list(prec = list(param = c(1, 1)),
                  dof  = list(initial=0, fixed = TRUE))
fix.hyper <- list(prec = 5e-1, prec.intercept = 5e-1)
a1.hyper <- list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1, 1e-02)))
t1.hyper <- list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(25, 5e-03)))

## Longitudinal linear regression with global and group-wise effects
fml <- y ~ 1 + t +
  f(a1, model = 'iid', hyper = a1.hyper) +
  f(t1, t, model = 'iid', hyper = t1.hyper)

## Model fit. With gaussian likelihood runs fine
## But T takes forever
res <- inla(fml,
            family = 'T',
            control.family = list(hyper = lik.hyper),
            control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
            control.fixed = fix.hyper,
            data = transform(dat,
                             y  = log(1 + p2d),
                             a1 = insee,
                             t1 = insee),
            verbose = TRUE)
​

messages.subject: request for hints on how to implement the spatio-temporal interpolation method of Saez et al 2012
messages.subject_clean: request for hints on how to implement the spatio-temporal interpolation method of Saez et al 2012
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am hoping to obtain perspectives by INLA experts on the method used by Saez et al 2012 (Space-time interpolation of daily air temperatures. J. Env Stat 3(5)) using INLA, and if favorable, to obtain some hints as to how one would implement it.

Specifically, on page 7 of their paper, they state:

For the final model estimation we used a two-stage approach. In the first stage, we assumed
the stations were spatially independent and we modeled the mean function of daily aver-
age temperatures controlling for possible temporal autocorrelation. In the second stage we
modeled the spatio-temporal covariance, using the interim posterior from the residuals of the
model (average within each cell) in the first stage as prior distributions of replications of a
spatial process.

When I attempted a spatio-temporal model with space-time separable assumption (as in the SPDE tutorial), model runs were extremely slow. Playing with different priors did not seem to help nor did reducing the size of the problem. I am thinking Saez et. al's method may speed up performance as the first stage can be made into a parallel process. And so, I would like to try it ...but ...how would one go about specifying the "priors distributions of replication"? Any hints or pointers would be greatly appreciated!

Best regards,
Jae

Mahmud

messages.subject: computing the distribution of the sum of predicted values over a spatial grid
messages.subject_clean: computing the distribution of the sum of predicted values over a spatial grid
messages.body_plain:
Dear inla group,
I have experienced some mismatch between predictions done by $summary.fitted.values and results from the inla.posterior.sample function when using the spde-inla model.
Actually I would like to compute the distribution of the sum of predicted values over a spatial grid. I used inla with the spde model (with two stack data combined: 'dat' and 'pred') and then used inla.posterior.sample in order to compute n samples from the posterior distribution. I sum the predict values from the 'latent' component at the 'pred' locations and I computed the distribution of my sum from the n samples.
The distribution of this sum was surprisingly always higher than the mean given by the sum of $summary.fitted.values at the 'pred' locations. At least the median (0.5 quantile) should be about the same, isn't it? All goes right when using a non-spatial model (without spde).

my code below:
stack.full <- inla.stack(stack.dat,stack.pred)

formulae <- (y~0+Intercept+X+f(spatial,model=spde))

mdl.inla <- inla(formulae, family="nbinomial", E=off7,
                        data = inla.stack.data(stack.full),
                        control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.full),compute=TRUE),quantiles=c(0.025,0.5,0.975),
                        control.results=list(return.marginals.random=FALSE,return.marginals.predictor=FALSE),
                        control.compute = list(dic=T,config=TRUE))

index.pred <- inla.stack.index(stack.full,tag="pred")$data

#expected mean sum
sum(exp(mdl.inla$summary.fitted.values[index.pred,1]+log(gridpred$off7)))

#posterior distribution of the sum
samples = inla.posterior.sample(1000,mdl.inla)
sum.pred <- vector("numeric",0)
for(i in 1:1000){
sum.pred[i] <- sum(exp(samples[[i]]$latent[index.pred]+log(gridpred$off7)))
}
quantile(sum.pred,c(0.025,0.5,0.975)) #0.5 quantile much higher than previous expected mean sum

All the best,
Kévin

On 28/10/14 14:58, Elias T Krainski wrote:

> predictor) setting the same link in both stack. For example
>    obs.stack <- inla.stack(data=list(..., link='log'), ...)
>    pred.stack <- inla.stack(data=list(..., link='log'), ...)
> best,

Normally, that would be  "link=1", which means "apply the link function
corresponding to the first likelihood".
The information also needs to be carried forward to the inla() call, as
well, via

   control.predictor=list( link=inla.stack.data(stack)$link )

This gives $summary.fitted.values with the link function applied to all
elements, not just the ones with data (this is discussed in the
r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> FAQ).  I'm however not sure what inla.posterior.sample()
does with this information.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I understand your concern about the linear predictor vs. response scale but both $summary.fitted.values and samples were at the the same scale with my code (linear predictor scale). If I use link=1, $summary.fitted.values becomes at the response scale but samples from inla.posterior.sample are still at the linear predictor scale. The sum of the mean of $summary.fitted.values is increased due to the exponential transformation but the sum of the median (0.5 quantile) is the same than before, which is expected. The difference between $summary.fitted.values and samples thus still occurs, at least when using spde term.

messages.subject: spatial model with multinomial distribution
messages.subject_clean: spatial model with multinomial distribution
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA,

I have a question about implementing the multinomial-poisson transform  with a spatial model.   If I implement the following multinomial approximation model:

formula = y ~ -1 +
   ## one intercept pr multinom observation
   f(idx, model="iid",
    hyper = list(
       prec = list(
       initial = log(0.000001),
       fixed = TRUE))) +
    f(jdx, x, model="iid",
        ## beta's sum to zero?
        constr = sum.to.zero,
        hyper = list(
        prec = list(
        initial = log(0.001),
        fixed = TRUE)))

Could one use the copy command to add a spatial random effect for each of the jdx groups in the Multinomial?  for example using something like that found in the DLM example  (http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/papers/DLM_examples_2011-10-23.R)?  Specifically, I'm looking at this part, which provides the temporal link between observations:

 + f(jdx, model="iid", initial=-10, fixed=T) +
   f(j, w1, copy="i")

Many thanks for the software and the help,

Tom

messages.subject: Re: request for hints on how to implement the spatio-temporal interpolation method of Saez et al 2012
messages.subject_clean: request for hints on how to implement the spatio-temporal interpolation method of Saez et al 2012
messages.body_plain:
So in case anyone else may be interested in the approach, Saez responded directed to me and explained that the temporal posteriors were added to the spatial model as an a-priori known component via an offset term (as it is an additive model).

He indicated that the approach requires high data density in space and time and so not as versatile as one might like and inefficient.

He instead recommended an approach based upon a 'misalignment' as in the spde tutorial. I think he meant running multiple time slices (after discretization?) with spatial parameters being shared across each slice as a 'copy' of each other.

So.. I think I'll just stick to the separable space-time approach for now.
